lesson.title: Interest on Interest: Compound Interest
lesson.summary: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original amount invested and on interest already earned, making an account balance grow exponentially rather than linearly, modeled by A equals P times (1 plus r over n) raised to the power n t.
lesson.body:
Simple interest pays a fixed dollar amount each period, always based on the original principal, so a balance earning simple interest grows linearly, adding the same amount every time. Compound interest is different and far more common in real banking and investing: it pays interest not only on the original principal but also on all interest already earned. That means the balance itself becomes the base for the next round of interest, which is exactly the multiply-by-a-constant-factor pattern from exponential growth. Each compounding period, the balance is multiplied by a growth factor greater than 1, just like in the growth factor chapter.

The compound interest formula is A equals P times (1 plus r over n) raised to the power n times t. Here A is the final amount, P is the principal, the initial value deposited, r is the annual interest rate written as a decimal, n is the number of times interest compounds per year, and t is the number of years. When interest compounds once a year, n equals 1, and the formula simplifies to A equals P times (1 plus r) raised to the t, which is the initial-value-and-growth-factor pattern you already know, with growth factor b equals 1 plus r.

Worked example 1, annual compounding: deposit 2,000 dollars at an annual rate of 5 percent, compounded once a year, for 3 years. Here P equals 2,000, r equals 0.05, n equals 1, and t equals 3, so A equals 2,000 times 1.05 raised to the 3. Compute 1.05 squared first: 1.05 times 1.05 equals 1.1025. Then multiply by 1.05 again: 1.1025 times 1.05 equals 1.157625. Finally, 2,000 times 1.157625 equals 2,315.25. So after 3 years the account holds 2,315.25 dollars, meaning 315.25 dollars of total interest was earned.

Worked example 2, comparing compounding frequency: deposit 1,000 dollars at 6 percent annual rate for 2 years, first compounded annually, then compounded monthly. Compounded annually, n equals 1: A equals 1,000 times 1.06 raised to the 2, and 1.06 times 1.06 equals 1.1236, so A equals 1,000 times 1.1236, which is 1,123.60 dollars. Compounded monthly, n equals 12: the rate per month is 0.06 divided by 12, which equals 0.005, and the number of periods is 12 times 2, which equals 24, so A equals 1,000 times 1.005 raised to the 24. Working that power out carefully gives 1.005 raised to the 24 is approximately 1.12716, so A is approximately 1,000 times 1.12716, which is about 1,127.16 dollars. Compounding monthly earned about 3.56 dollars more than compounding annually, even though the nominal annual rate of 6 percent was exactly the same in both cases, because the interest itself started earning interest sooner and more often.

Compound interest is one of the clearest real-world examples of exponential growth: money grows by a constant percentage of the current balance, not a constant dollar amount, which is precisely the comparison explored in the upcoming chapter on linear versus exponential growth.
